page.title: Working Student at Vector
page.metaDescription: This page describes the working student position developer Denis Mathan held at Vector, in software development.
intro: As a working student in software development at Vector, I worked on a SharePoint web part that visualizes an organization's structure.
I built a new diagram view of the organization using ReactFlow, alongside a table-based view, both dynamically driven by data configured in SharePoint.

A big part of the work went into an editor for the underlying data. Before it existed, updating the displayed structure meant going through a lengthy git-merge process, and the same information was often duplicated redundantly across separate JSON files for different organizations. The editor addresses this: it writes directly into the JSON files stored in a SharePoint folder, using a checkout/check-in mechanism to avoid conflicts — and if a conflict does happen anyway, the user can choose which change to keep. It also supports undo/redo, and shows a live preview of how unpushed changes would look in the other views. Migration scripts consolidate the old, per-organization JSON files into a single global data file.

page.title: Experience at Valueminer
page.metaDescription: This page describes the time that developer Denis Mathan experienced at Valueminer.
intro: In simplified terms, Valueminer sells a web-based management program that can be customized to meet customer requirements using low-code. In theory, it's a highly dynamic tool, limited only by the imagination of its users. In practice, those ideas still need to be built before they can be configured.

My contributions there included several new dashboard widgets (charts, heatmaps, a machine-transfer widget, and more), a CO2 calculator built on top of the OpenAI API, and a persistence layer (a kind of memory) for the app. I also built the full Firebird-to-Valueminer converter from scratch — it can itself be configured via JSON, though the JSON-configuration side wasn't something I worked on directly. On top of that came a steady stream of general bugfixing.
My tools there included AWS, Docker, Angular with TypeScript, and Golang on the backend.

page.title: Tutor App
page.metaDescription: This page presents a tutoring-platform application built by developer Denis Mathan as part of a team project.
intro: A Java Spring Boot application that lets students sign up for tutoring sessions against payment. The system distinguishes between three roles — Admin, Tutor, and Student — each with their own permissions.

Within the team, I was responsible for most of the core account and security infrastructure: OAuth login via Google, email/password authentication, two-factor authentication, email verification, password hashing with BCrypt, the email service, and the overall security chain. A teammate handled the PayPal integration.

The biggest takeaway from this project wasn't technical, though: working with an unfamiliar, distributed team taught me just how much a solid, automated test suite tied into the git merge workflow can save you.

programming.name: Hits & History

page.title: Hits & History
page.metaDescription: This page presents Hits & History, a data warehousing project by developer Denis Mathan examining the link between world events and music charts.
intro: Hits & History looks at whether crisis and conflict data from around the world left any trace in the German, British, and American music charts — combining datasets from EM-DAT (disasters) and the Global Terrorism Database with German charts (self-scraped) and British/American charts (from Kaggle).

A fair share of the work went into data cleaning — for example, the British chart data had a recurring encoding bug that stripped every 're' from song titles. Every song across all charts was then enriched via the MusicBrainz API, at a rate of about one request per second — roughly a week of runtime in total.
In the end, no clear causal relationship between world events and chart performance emerged — but the project produced some genuinely nice visualizations in Power BI.

programming.name: Quantum Computing Fundamentals
description: A scientific paper on the potential of quantum computing for classical computational problems.
Covers Grover's and Shor's algorithms and where they sit within complexity theory.

page.title: Quantum Computing Fundamentals
page.metaDescription: This page presents a scientific paper by developer Denis Mathan on the potential of quantum computing for classical computational problems.
intro: A scientific paper, written in LaTeX, examining what quantum computing can offer for classical computational problems — centered on Grover's and Shor's algorithms and the complexity classes P, NP, BPP, and BQP.

The result: Grover's algorithm gives a quadratic speedup, while Shor's algorithm (via the Quantum Fourier Transform) gives an exponential one. However, integer factorization is not known to be NP-complete — so this doesn't shake the boundaries of classical complexity theory.

page.title: ML Diabetes Prediction
page.metaDescription: This page presents a scientific paper by developer Denis Mathan comparing machine learning models for diabetes detection.
intro: A scientific paper examining how well different machine learning models can detect diabetes, applying each of them to four different datasets.

The models compared were Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, K-Nearest Neighbors, and neural networks — with the central question being which of these models perform well on which kind of dataset.

programming.name: Grimlang
description: An interpreter for a self-designed programming language whose syntax reads like a fairy tale.
Parses the fairytale-style syntax into an AST and executes it.

page.title: Grimlang
page.metaDescription: This page presents Grimlang, an interpreted programming language designed by developer Denis Mathan whose syntax reads like a fairy tale.
intro: Grimlang is a small interpreted programming language I designed and built myself, written in C, with one specific goal: its syntax should read less like code and more like a fairy tale.

Keywords are drawn from storytelling — a function is a "Kapitel" (chapter), a print statement is "las" (told), a return is "Gib alles!" (give everything!), and conditionals read as "Wenn ... gilt ... Ansonsten ..." (if ... then ... otherwise ...). Under the hood, the source is parsed with Bison into an AST and then interpreted.
Here's what a small Grimlang program looks like:

Kapitel UmpaLumpa.
 las "In Funktion2 passiert nicht viel...", "\n".
 Gib alles!
 Ende!

 Kapitel Schlacht
 handelt von Held namens A und Held namens B.
 las "In Funktion: A: ", A," B: ", B, " test", "\n".
 Ende!

 Kapitel fakultät
 handelt von Held namens A.
 Gib alles 3!
 Wenn A anders als 1 ist, gilt:
 //Gib alles 1!
 Es gab einen Helden namens B.
 B war so stark wie A und -1 zusammen.
 las "Test: ", A, "\n".
 Gib alles A mal In Kapitel fakultät mehr Abenteuer von B zu finden!
 Ansonsten: Gib alles 1!
 Verstanden?
 Ende!
